notes: From Poland: Stanislaw Pyzik puts the postwar settlers at 20,000-22,000; the Polish community priest cited by the Circulo Polones says about 16,000; a net-migration series gives 16,784 for 1941-50. Over 20,000 Polish citizens arrived but about 9,000 were registered as Poles. Source: Circulo Polones, 'La tercera ola de inmigracion polaca 1946-1950' (https://circulopolones.com.ar/la-tercera-ola-de-inmigracion-polaca-1946-1950/); 'Polonia argentynska', historia.org.pl (https://historia.org.pl/2012/10/03/polonia-argentynska/).

From Poland: Growth of the Poland-born population of Australia between the 1947 and 1954 censuses (about 50,000), mostly post-war displaced persons. Split evenly by year over 1947-54, so 3/8 of it falls here; the real arrivals were concentrated around 1948-51. Net of deaths and departures, so it understates arrivals. Source: Australian census Poland-born counts: 1947 about 6,573 and 1954 about 56,600 (ABS 1947 census birthplace volume; secondary sources Wikipedia 'Polish Australians' and the Polish Council of Australia).

From Poland: Wspolnota Polska gives 10,000-20,000 Poles in the first postwar years (1,481 displaced Poles from mid-1947 to mid-1948 and 7,397 by March 1950); another source gives about 30,000 for 1945-50. The Memorial do Imigrante records show 4,718 Poles entering São Paulo's hostel in 1947-51 (26% of 18,369 arrivals), 9% of whom later applied for exit visas, mostly for the United States. Source: Wspolnota Polska, 'Polacy i osoby polskiego pochodzenia w Brazylii' (https://wspolnotapolska.org.pl/biblioteka/bib_artykuly.php?id=15%2F); Senia Bastos and Maria do Rosario Rolfsen Salles, 'A imigracao polonesa para Sao Paulo no pos-Segunda Guerra Mundial', Revista Brasileira de Estudos de Populacao (https://www.scielo.br/j/rbepop/a/qW6Xfrqt7ZnYWN9ZmyxryVS/).

From Poland: Official annual counts 1946: 398, 1947: 4,655, 1948: 27,741, 1949: 20,091. 1945 is not covered by the source table (total immigration to Canada that year was far lower than in 1946-49), so this period has four years and probably understates slightly. Poland was the largest source in 1948-50 after the British Isles and the US. Cross-check: Canada Year Book 1963-64 gives 93,827 from Poland for 1946-62, which these annual figures sum to. Source: Statistics Canada, Canada Year Book 1951, p. 143, table 2 (immigrant admissions by country of last permanent residence, 1946-49).

To Poland: More than 12,000 men were interned (some sources say over 13,000). When internment ended about 2,000 went home despite a strong repatriation campaign by Polish communists in Switzerland, about 9,000 moved to France, and about 1,000-1,300 stayed in Switzerland (around 500 later took Swiss citizenship). The claim that more than half of the division went home is contradicted by both the IPN article and dzieje.pl, which say most did not return. Source: Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), 'Z ziemi helweckiej do polskiej', https://przystanekhistoria.pl/pa2/tematy/polskie-wojsko/69993,Z-ziemi-helweckiej-do-polskiej.html; Poland in Exile, 'The Polish Army in France & 2DSP Internment in Switzerland', https://polandinexile.com/en/article/the-polish-army-in-france-2dsp-internment-in-switzerland-1939-1940/; dzieje.pl, https://dzieje.pl/node/152006.

To Poland: Repatriates and reemigrants arriving from Czechoslovakia through the western PUR stations, July 1946 to December 1947: 1,536 (repatriates 1,201 + reemigrants 335); of these 872 in 1947 (551 + 321), so 664 in Jul-Dec 1946. The yearbook gives no country split for Jul-Dec 1945, Jan-Jun 1946 or 1948, when most of the movement through Czechoslovakia took place (the western stations received 656,182 people in Jul-Dec 1945 alone, mostly from Germany). A history blog quotes 14,502 arrivals from Czechoslovakia for 1945-47 at one station (Dziedzice) without naming a source; it was not verified and is not used, but it suggests that the true total is many times higher. Jiří Friedl's monograph on Poland's citizens in Czechoslovakia 1945-48 has the full numbers and was not available. Source: GUS, Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, Table 5B 'Repatriacja i reemigracja do Polski przez punkty etapowe zachodnie PUR, według krajów (VII 1946 - XII 1947)', p. 28 (source: Państwowy Urząd Repatriacyjny), https://statlibr.stat.gov.pl/exlibris/aleph/a22_1/apache_media/SFGFA59FBIX2KUU9ER34EY9RMJ7TC8.pdf.

From Poland: Czechs and Slovaks who reemigrated from Poland to Czechoslovakia by the end of 1949, from the final report on the mass reemigration of Czechs and Slovaks from abroad (National Archive Prague, fond MPSP-R 1938-1951, carton 538). For comparison the same report gives, from other countries: USSR 42,580, Hungary 65,334, Romania 21,001, France 12,915, Austria 11,117, Yugoslavia 5,197, Germany 4,059. This is nationality-based (Czech or Slovak ethnicity) and counts to the end of 1949, so it covers the whole 1945-49 period, but includes people from the Czech enclaves in the Polish-held border areas and does not include the Poles' side of the exchange. Source: Martin Nedvěd, Nemajetní krajané - plus pro stranu? Vliv KSČ na poválečnou reemigraci, Právněhistorické studie 53(2), 2023, pp. 147-158, footnote 30, quoting the archival report, https://karolinum.cz/data/clanek/11869/PHS_53_2_0147.pdf.

To Poland: Kersten (1974) puts repatriation from Germany in 1945-50 at 1,642,500, from other European countries at 298,500 and from outside Europe at 8,000 (about 1.95 million in all, excluding people moved from the former eastern territories). Organised repatriation from the Western zones, from her Table 15: to 1 January 1946: 196,585 from the American zone, 14,933 from the French and 155,845 from the British; during 1946: 130,605, 26,517 and 200,816; January to June 1947: 26,258, 3,563 and 12,625; July 1947 to August 1948 (as printed): 10,731, 1,437 and 13,818; in all 364,179, 46,450 and 383,104 = 793,733 (plus 71,904 from Austria). About 700,000 Polish forced labourers and prisoners of war were in the Soviet zone at the end of the war. At the end of September 1945 there were still 816,012 Poles in the Western zones (Proudfoot, cited by Knapton), and Polish repatriation from there slowed to 79,932 between December 1945 and March 1946. This replaces the earlier midpoint of 1.5 to 2 million. Source: Krystyna Kersten, Repatriacja ludnosci polskiej po II wojnie swiatowej (Wroclaw 1974), as cited by Konkret24, https://konkret24.tvn24.pl/polityka/wybory-2023-morawiecki-polacy-pierwszy-raz-od-200-lat-masowo-wracaja-z-emigracji-nie-ma-na-to-danych-st7364192; Urszula Kurcewicz, Acta Universitatis Lodziensis, Folia Historica 117 (2024), Table 15 after Kersten pp. 216-217, https://czasopisma.uni.lodz.pl/historica/article/download/25775/25605; Samantha K. Knapton, European History Quarterly 50(4) (2020), https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/75580/7/Published_Version.pdf.

From Poland: Organised expulsions by year (Polish Ministry of the Interior data, Nitschke): 1946: 1,620,610 (1,192,788 to the British zone, 427,822 to the Soviet zone); 1947: about 536,000 (the ministries' figures run from 534,961 to 572,529); 1948: 49,145; 1949: 65,520. Jankowiak (IPN) gives 2,189,286 Germans in 1,337 transports from the start of the action to 31 December 1947, against about 2,157,000 for 1946-47 here. Another 60,000 or so left in 1950 and about 150,000 Germans in 1950-59; those are not in this period. The Allied Control Council plan of 20 November 1945 foresaw 3.5 million, and Sienkiewicz and Hryciuk's atlas is cited at 3.092 million Germans moved from Poland in 1945-50 (Hrynicki and Widerski). German-side totals for people who arrived from all the eastern territories are higher because they include the pre-war German provinces and other countries. Source: Bernadetta Nitschke, 'Wysiedlenia i wyjazdy ludnosci niemieckiej z Polski w latach 1945-1959', Studia Zachodnie 3 (1998), https://zbc.uz.zgora.pl/Content/45907/PDF/14_nitschke_wysiedlenia.pdf; Stanislaw Jankowiak, 'Wysiedlenia Niemcow z Polski po II wojnie swiatowej', Pamiec i Sprawiedliwosc 3/2 (2004), https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/pamiec-i-sprawiedliwosc/2004-tom-3-numer-2-6/pamiec_i_sprawiedliwosc-r2004-t3-n2_6-s139-160.pdf; Wojciech Hrynicki and Jaroslaw Widerski, Kultura Bezpieczenstwa 24 (2016), https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/kultura-bezpieczenstwa-nauka-praktyka-refleksje/2016-numer-24/kultura_bezpieczenstwa_nauka_praktyka_refleksje-r2016-t-n24-s92-117.pdf.

To Poland: Polish count to the end of 1948: about 58,000; the French count is about 51,000. Pawel Sekowski gives almost 70,000 for 1946-48, and the 1950 Polish census recorded 78,400 returnees from France (Dzieciuchowicz 2000), the same 78,000 by the end of 1950 (the last two years are doubted, because reemigration had stalled). Janine Ponty gives about 50,000 (French) and nearly 80,000 (Polish) and calls both contested. The French census counted 423,470 Poles in March 1946 and 269,269 in 1954, a fall that also reflects naturalisation and deaths. Source: Grzegorz Pelczynski, 'Losy reemigrantow z Francji w okresie PRL i III RP', Studia Migracyjne - Przeglad Polonijny 2/2019 (https://ejournals.eu/pliki_artykulu_czasopisma/pelny_tekst/92bc8ed7-dabb-4bc7-8eb9-4e52a6ecc4a2/pobierz); Pawel Sekowski, Dzieje Najnowsze 2/2014 (http://rcin.org.pl/Content/47194/PDF/WA303_63632_A507-DN-R-46-2_Sekowski.pdf); Jerzy Dzieciuchowicz, 'Polonia francuska', Acta Universitatis Lodziensis, Folia Geographica Socio-Oeconomica 3/2000 (https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/acta-universitatis-lodziensis-folia-geographica-socio-oeconomica/2000-numer-3/acta_universitatis_lodziensis_folia_geographica_socio_oeconomica-r2000-t-n3-s31-57.pdf); Janine Ponty, 'Les rapatriements d'ouvriers polonais (1945-1948)' (https://pbc.uw.edu.pl/24175/1/Ponty.pdf); INSEE 1999 census retrospective table R6 (https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/2118512).

From Poland: 114,000 Poles joined the Polish Resettlement Corps (formed September 1946) instead of returning to Poland; about 78,000 were in civilian jobs by January 1949, about 20,000 had emigrated or been repatriated and about 14,600 were still to be resettled. The Polish Resettlement Act 1947 allowed more than 220,000 Poles with dependants to stay. Source: Hansard, written answers 25 January 1949, Polish Resettlement Corps (https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written-answers/1949/jan/25/polish-resettlement-corps); National Archives blog on the 1947 Act.

To Poland: 1,013 + 2,092 = 3,105 children, from Nowicka. The IPN volume gives 'more than 3,000 children' evacuated, which agrees. Replaces an earlier 12,000 from Wikipedia that put all refugees in 1945-49. Source: Ewa Nowicka, Forced Emigration and Desired Return: The Social and Psychological Consequences of the Wartime Evacuation of Greeks, Balcanica Posnaniensia XXIV (2017), https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/bp/article/view/6857.

To Poland: Poles returning from Hungary: 1945: about 25,000; 1946: 834; 1947: 221; 1948: 28; 1949: 36 (1950: 35). Figures are attributed to Kersten (1974, pp. 237-238) in the article; the 1945 value is rounded. The Polish legation's consular reports give different numbers: 141 for the last two months of 1946 only, and 316 (1947), 90 (1948), 80 (1949), 4 (1950); the author warns that they mix repatriates and reemigrants. Historians put the number of Poles in Hungary at 50,000 to 140,000. Nothing was found on Hungarian refugees or other flows to Poland in 1956. Source: Aleksandra Sylburska, Repatriacja/reemigracja Polaków z Węgier po zakończeniu II wojny światowej, Prace Historyczne 148(2), 2021, pp. 411-423, quoting K. Kersten, Repatriacja ludności polskiej po II wojnie światowej, Wrocław 1974, https://ejournals.eu/pliki_artykulu_czasopisma/pelny_tekst/4fde003f-8047-46b7-923a-9bba94481226/pobierz.

From Poland: CBS gives 106,414 for 1948-51; split evenly by year, so 1948-49 get half. Arrivals before the state (1945-47) are not in the table. Counts people born in Poland, not necessarily arriving from Poland. Source: Central Bureau of Statistics (Israel), Statistical Abstract of Israel 2010, Table 4.4 (immigrants by period of immigration and country of birth).

From Poland: Polish displaced persons resettled in New Zealand in 1949-51 (about 744), split evenly by year, so 1/3 falls here. The census agrees (Poland-born residents rose by about 700 between 1945 and 1951). The 733 children and 105 adults of the Pahiatua group arrived in 1944, before this timeline starts. Under 1,000 people, so no line is drawn on the map. Source: Kresy-Siberia, 'Polish Refugees in New Zealand 1944-1951' (about 744 Poles among about 4,500 displaced persons, 1949-51); Te Ara 'Poles' (census Poland-born 1,307 in 1945 and 2,003 in 1951).

To Poland: Two non-overlapping windows added: 3,075 war refugees who left Romania for Poland from June 1945 to April 1946 (Nowak, citing Sowińska-Krupka 1985), and 4,208 people (371 repatriates + 3,837 reemigrants) who arrived from Romania through the western PUR stations between July 1946 and December 1947 (3,545 of them in 1947: 260 + 3,285; GUS Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 5B). The PUR figure fits Nowak's transports: 503 people in September 1946 and a further 3,403 by mid-July 1947 (770 of them war refugees and pre-war labour emigrants, the rest mostly from Southern Bukovina). Nowak also gives 4,858 former Romanian citizens who left in 1946-1950 in all (the last transport at the end of April 1950); the remainder for 1948-49 would be about 1,000 (4,858 minus 3,837 reemigrants) if the groups match, which was not verified and is not added. May-June 1946 is not covered by either window. A regional article's 45,000 Poles leaving 'Bukovina' in 1945-47 is not used: Bukovina was split between Romania and the Soviet Union, and that figure is not broken down. Source: Krzysztof Nowak, Reemigracja polskich górników z Rumunii na Górny Śląsk po II wojnie światowej, Śląski Kwartalnik Historyczny Sobótka 73(4), 2018, pp. 77-102, https://www.repozytorium.uni.wroc.pl/Content/132960/PDF/04_K_Nowak_Reemigracja_polskich_gornikow_z_Rumunii.pdf; GUS, Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 5B (source: Państwowy Urząd Repatriacyjny), p. 28, https://statlibr.stat.gov.pl/exlibris/aleph/a22_1/apache_media/SFGFA59FBIX2KUU9ER34EY9RMJ7TC8.pdf.

To Poland: Arrivals in Poland from USSR territory, by year: 1945: 723,488; 1946: 644,437; 1947: 10,801 (PUR, GUS Rocznik 1948 table 6, which totals 1,495,938 for Oct 1944 to 1947 with 117,212 in 1944); 1948: 7,325 (repatriations, Bartoszewicz citing GUS Rocznik 1949). Sum 1,386,051. Excluded: 117,212 arrivals in 1944, and 22,815 more who came by road during the whole action (the table's footnote). Table 6 splits the total into resettled from the Ukrainian, Belarusian and Lithuanian SSRs (787,600 + 274,163 + 178,013) and repatriated from the rest of the USSR (256,162); Bartoszewicz gives 1,503,263 for 1944-48, which equals the table's 1,495,938 plus 7,325 and confirms it. 1949 is not included (no figure found). Earlier cell: 1.1 million from Wikipedia, then 1,503,263 which included 1944. Source: GUS, Rocznik Statystyczny 1948, table 6 'Repatriacja z Z.S.R.R. do Polski', p. 28 (source: Państwowy Urząd Repatriacyjny), https://statlibr.stat.gov.pl/exlibris/aleph/a22_1/apache_media/SFGFA59FBIX2KUU9ER34EY9RMJ7TC8.pdf; 1948 from Henryk Bartoszewicz, Przegląd Historyczny 87(3), 1996, p. 572, https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/przeglad-historyczny/1996-tom-87-numer-3/przeglad_historyczny-r1996-t87-n3-s563-578.pdf.

From Poland: Ukrainians resettled to the Ukrainian SSR from 15 Oct 1944 to the end of 1946: 487,398 (273,330 from Rzeszów, 193,975 from Lublin, 20,093 from Kraków voivodeship); 221,321 of them by 3 Sep 1945, the rest by the army groups to 13 Jul 1946. A search summary of a Ukrainian article gave 488,057 for the same period (not opened). Operation Vistula (1947) moved people inside Poland and is not counted. Belarusians and Lithuanians resettled to their own SSRs are not in this figure. Source: Roman Drozd, Zasady rozmieszczenia ludności ukraińskiej na Ziemiach Odzyskanych w ramach akcji Wisła, Słupskie Studia Historyczne 3, 1993, pp. 97-112 (citing Szczęśniak and Szota, Droga do nikąd; CAW Sztab Generalny WP), https://bazhum.muzhp.pl/media/texts/supskie-studia-historyczne/1993-tom-3/slupskie_studia_historyczne-r1993-t3-s97-112.pdf.

From Poland: Official annual counts, FY1945: 40, 1946: 806, 1947: 8,156, 1948: 8,020, 1949: 23,744. FY1945-46 come from a badly scanned table and are small; the period is dominated by FY1949 (Displaced Persons Act, from mid-1948). Source: US Immigration and Naturalization Service, Annual Report 1953 (table 33A, immigrants admitted by country or region of birth, FY1944-53) and 1957.

To Poland: Poles (old settlers and their families, mostly from northern Bosnia around Banja Luka, a few from Croatia, Serbia and Slovenia) resettled to Poland under the Polish-Yugoslav protocol of 2 Jan 1946: 32 transports from 28 Mar to 5 Nov 1946, most of them settled in Bolesławiec County (Lower Silesia). The Mixed Commission's final protocol of 3 Nov 1946 gives 15,301 persons. Families: 2,930 (Baniecki, AP Wrocław) vs 3,924 (Oliwa); not resolved. PUR reports that include a 33rd transport (78 families, Banja Luka; the AP page says about 100 families in Sep 1947) and individual arrivals give about 20,000 by the end of 1948 (rounded; Oliwa also uses 'almost 20,000' for the county alone). About 2,000 Poles stayed in Yugoslavia. A search summary quoted 14,088 to 18,000 for Bosnia (Wikipedia, not used). Kamberović (Časopis za suvremenu povijest 30, 1998) has the Yugoslav side but its PDF could not be downloaded. Source: Mieczysław Oliwa, Osadnictwo w powiecie bolesławieckim po II wojnie światowej, Studia z zakresu nauk prawnoustrojowych, Miscellanea 10, 2020, pp. 86-88 (citing AP Wrocław, PUR, sygn. 627, 1216), https://kpsw.edu.pl/pobierz/wydawnictwo/Miscellanea/T_%20X/Oliwa.pdf; Adam Baniecki, Osadnictwo Polaków z byłej Jugosławii w powiecie bolesławieckim 1946-1947 (AP Wrocław, PUR sygn. 794), https://www.wroclaw.ap.gov.pl/odcienie-regionalizmu/b_repzjug.html.

From Poland: Growth of the Poland-born population of Australia between the 1947 and 1954 censuses (about 50,000), mostly post-war displaced persons. From Poland: Official annual counts 1950: 9,747, 1951: 14,245, 1952: 3,358, 1953: 136, 1954: 45. Emigration from Poland was almost entirely blocked in 1953-56, hence the near-zero counts. Source: Statistics Canada, Canada Year Book 1956, p. 182 (1950-54) and 1957-58 (1952-56), immigrant admissions by country of last permanent residence.

From Poland: Ethnic Germans to the Federal Republic, 1950-54, after the big expulsions; only 1950 (31,761) and 1951 (10,791) were sizeable. Annual: 1950: 31,761, 1951: 10,791, 1952: 194, 1953: 147, 1954: 662. Ethnic Germans only: Polish citizens leaving for Germany are not counted before 1974. Source: Bundesverwaltungsamt, (Spaet-)Aussiedler und ihre Angehoerigen, Zeitreihe 1950-2014 by country of origin (Poland), https://www.mi.niedersachsen.de/download/100095/Zeitreihe_1950_-_2014_Spaetaussiedler_und_ihre_Angehoerigen.pdf.

From Poland: The 1971 census counted 13,470 Poland-born residents of Great Britain who had arrived in 1950-71 (75% women). Allowing for arrivals who had died or left by 1971, gross arrivals are assumed to be about 15,000 over 1950-71, so about 13,600 for 1950-69, split evenly over the four periods. Source: 1971 census total as quoted in J. Hanson, PhD thesis, University of Sheffield, 1995 (https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/14465/1/364384Vol1.pdf, p. 29); the census table of year of entry by country of birth (Country of Birth Tables 1974, p. 128) could not be obtained.

To Poland: Adults came from 16 December 1949 (Zgorzelec) and in 1950 (Nowicka). Other totals: 12,300 for 1948-51 and about 15,000 (secondary sources found by search, not read). Source: Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), PRL a wojna domowa w Grecji / The Polish People's Republic and the Greek Civil War (ed. M. Semczyszyn, Szczecin 2016), publisher's summary, https://ipn.gov.pl/pl/wydawnictwo/do-pobrania/publikacje-obcojezyczne/233032,PRL-a-wojna-domowa-w-Grecji-The-Polish-Peoples-Republic-and-the-Greek-Civil-War.pdf.

From Poland: The other half of the CBS 1948-51 total (1950-51). Nothing is added for 1952-54, when emigration was effectively closed. Counts people born in Poland, not necessarily arriving from Poland. Source: Central Bureau of Statistics (Israel), Statistical Abstract of Israel 2010, Table 4.4 (immigrants by period of immigration and country of birth).

From Poland: Polish displaced persons resettled in New Zealand in 1949-51 (about 744), split evenly by year, so 2/3 falls here. To Poland: Individual returns from the USSR with Soviet passports and family reunification: about 1,600 in 1950-52 (MSZ), 1,096 in 1953 and 2,017 in 1954 (Biuletyn Informacyjny o Repatriacji); 4,713 in all. Two sources disagree on 1954: MSZ says about 400, which would give 3,096 for the period. Extras that may or may not be in these counts: 787 children by July 1952, 308 released from camps in 1951 (260 in March, 48 in September), a group of 358 under the amnesty on 9 Jan 1954. Later in the series: 6,429 by Oct 1955, which belongs to 1955-59. Cross-check: IPN gives 10,000 to 20,000 for all of 1948-55, and 7,325 (1948, Bartoszewicz) + 4,713 + 6,429 (1955 to Oct) is already 18,467 before 1949, so the three fit. No mass repatriation took place in these years; the borderland resettlement ended in 1946 and the Soviet side closed the question in the late 1940s. Source: Ewelina Iwona Rytelewska, Prawne i polityczne aspekty przemieszczeń ludności polskiej z ZSRR, Studia Prawnoustrojowe 63, 2024, pp. 371-372 (citing AMSZ Zespół 7 via A. Paczkowski, Powrót żołnierzy AK z sowieckich łagrów, 1995, and the Biuletyn Informacyjny o Repatriacji), https://czasopisma.uwm.edu.pl/index.php/sp/article/download/9419/7379/35490.

From Poland: Official annual counts, FY1950: 52,851, 1951: 37,484, 1952: 33,211, 1953: 4,395, 1954: 5,663. Admissions under the Displaced Persons Acts (1948-52) and the Refugee Relief Act (1953-56): by last residence these Poles appear as Germany or Austria, which is why the earlier last-residence figures were far too low. Source: US Immigration and Naturalization Service, Annual Reports 1950, 1952, 1953 and 1957 (immigrants admitted by country or region of birth).

From Poland: Modelled net inflow of Poland-born people to Australia: change in the Poland-born population plus assumed deaths, spread evenly by year. Deaths use an annual mortality rate of 0.3% rising to 1.9% as the cohort ages, set at half my first guess because the ABS data for 2005-2020 imply 2.1-2.6%. Emigration and return are not subtracted, so this is a net figure; the mortality rates are assumptions, not data. Source: Modelled from Poland-born counts in Australia (ABS Historical Population Statistics table 5.37: census counts 1954, 1961, 1971, 1981; UN DESA estimates for 1990 to 2005) plus deaths at a mortality rate calibrated to the ABS 2005-2020 data.

From Poland: Official annual counts 1955: 113, 1956: 186, 1957: 690, 1958: 2,292, 1959: 3,470. Source: Statistics Canada, Canada Year Book 1957-58 (1955-56), 1959 p. 179 (1953-57) and 1962 p. 164 (1957-61), immigrant admissions by country of last permanent residence.

bases.m: Growth of the Poland-born population of Australia between the 1947 and 1954 censuses (about 50,000), split evenly by year.
bases.w: Arrivals were concentrated around 1948-51 and the figure is net of deaths, so the even split and the net basis both distort it.

bases.s: Krystyna Kersten, Repatriacja ludnosci polskiej po II wojnie swiatowej (Wroclaw 1974), as cited by Konkret24, https://konkret24.tvn24.pl/polityka/wybory-2023-morawiecki-polacy-pierwszy-raz-od-200-lat-masowo-wracaja-z-emigracji-nie-ma-na-to-danych-st7364192; Urszula Kurcewicz, Acta Universitatis Lodziensis, Folia Historica 117 (2024), Table 15 after Kersten pp. 216-217, https://czasopisma.uni.lodz.pl/historica/article/download/25775/25605; Samantha K. Knapton, European History Quarterly 50(4) (2020), https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/75580/7/Published_Version.pdf
bases.m: Poles returning to Poland from Germany (forced labourers, prisoners of war, concentration-camp survivors and displaced persons), 1945-1950, as counted by the historian Krystyna Kersten; practically all returns were in 1945-48.
bases.w: Only about half is registered: the organised repatriation from the three Western zones was 793,733 (to August 1948). bases.m: Polish workers and their families who returned from France to Poland under the Franco-Polish reemigration agreements (convoys from May 1946 to December 1948), taken as the Polish count to the end of 1948.
bases.w: The counts conflict (51,000 French, 58,000 Polish, almost 70,000 in Sekowski, 78,000 to the end of 1950), France did not record every departure, and the figures cover the old labour emigration only, not the repatriation of displaced persons.

bases.s: Circulo Polones, 'La tercera ola de inmigracion polaca 1946-1950' (https://circulopolones.com.ar/la-tercera-ola-de-inmigracion-polaca-1946-1950/); 'Polonia argentynska', historia.org.pl (https://historia.org.pl/2012/10/03/polonia-argentynska/)
bases.m: Estimated number of Poles who settled in Argentina in the postwar wave of 1946-50 (mostly soldiers of the Polish forces and their families, and displaced persons), taken as the lower end of a published range of 20,000 to 22,000.
bases.w: No official count by nationality exists: estimates range from 16,000 to 22,000, many arrivals travelled on British or IRO papers and only about 9,000 were registered as Polish, and the wave ran to 1950 while the period ends in 1949.

bases.s: Wspolnota Polska, 'Polacy i osoby polskiego pochodzenia w Brazylii' (https://wspolnotapolska.org.pl/biblioteka/bib_artykuly.php?id=15%2F); Senia Bastos and Maria do Rosario Rolfsen Salles, 'A imigracao polonesa para Sao Paulo no pos-Segunda Guerra Mundial', Revista Brasileira de Estudos de Populacao (https://www.scielo.br/j/rbepop/a/qW6Xfrqt7ZnYWN9ZmyxryVS/)
bases.m: Estimated number of Poles who arrived in Brazil in the first postwar years, taken as the lower end of a published range of 10,000 to 20,000.
bases.w: No national count by nationality was found: estimates range from 10,000 to 30,000 for 1945-50, the only archive count (4,718 Poles, 1947-51) covers São Paulo's immigrant hostel records alone, and many displaced persons moved on to the United States and Canada.

bases.s: Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), 'Z ziemi helweckiej do polskiej', https://przystanekhistoria.pl/pa2/tematy/polskie-wojsko/69993,Z-ziemi-helweckiej-do-polskiej.html; Poland in Exile, 'The Polish Army in France & 2DSP Internment in Switzerland', https://polandinexile.com/en/article/the-polish-army-in-france-2dsp-internment-in-switzerland-1939-1940/; dzieje.pl, https://dzieje.pl/node/152006
bases.m: Polish soldiers of the 2nd Rifle Division interned in Switzerland since 1940 who went back to Poland when the internment ended in 1945 (the repatriation ran from 8 May to 15 December 1945).
bases.w: A round figure of about 2,000 that comes from one line in Polish secondary writing (it probably traces to Matyja's 2013 monograph, which I could not read). It covers soldiers only, not civilians, and excludes the many who moved on from France to Poland later.

bases.s: Ewa Nowicka, Forced Emigration and Desired Return: The Social and Psychological Consequences of the Wartime Evacuation of Greeks, Balcanica Posnaniensia XXIV (2017), https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/bp/article/view/6857
bases.m: Greek and Macedonian children evacuated from the Greek Civil War to Poland: two rail transports in September-October 1948 (1,013) and groups in April 1949 (2,092).
bases.w: Only the children's transports are dated; the adult refugees are not counted here (the first adult group reached Zgorzelec on 16 December 1949), so this is a lower bound for 1945-49. Refugees, not migrants by choice, and not Greeks moving from Greece in a statistical sense.

bases.s: Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), PRL a wojna domowa w Grecji / The Polish People's Republic and the Greek Civil War (ed. M. Semczyszyn, Szczecin 2016), publisher's summary, https://ipn.gov.pl/pl/wydawnictwo/do-pobrania/publikacje-obcojezyczne/233032,PRL-a-wojna-domowa-w-Grecji-The-Polish-Peoples-Republic-and-the-Greek-Civil-War.pdf
bases.m: Greek Civil War refugees (Greeks and Macedonians) who reached Poland from the end of 1949 and in the 1950s: the IPN total of 'more than 13,000' minus the 3,105 children counted under 1945-49.
bases.w: A lower bound derived by subtraction from one total whose period split is not published. It assumes the IPN total includes the children; the English summary says 'in addition more than 3,000 children', which would make the adult figure about 13,000. Some adults came with the children before 1950. Nowicka gives about 20,000 refugees in all, probably counting those born in Poland.

bases.s: Statistik Austria, Wanderungen mit dem Ausland (Außenwanderungen) 2002-2025 nach Herkunfts- bzw. Zielland (Tabellensammlung, sheet T5, https://www.statistik.at/statistiken/bevoelkerung-und-soziales/bevoelkerung/migration-und-einbuergerung/wanderungen-mit-dem-ausland), Poland as country of origin or destination
bases.m: People registered as moving between the country and Poland, all citizenships, summed over the calendar years of the period. Gross counts: immigrants include Austrians returning from Poland, and emigrants include Poles going home; moves with unknown origin or destination (5-33% of Wegzuege, 33% in 2002, 12% in 2010, 5% in 2024) are not counted under Poland, so both are lower bounds.

bases.s: Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), Wanderungsstatistik: Zuzuege and Fortzuege between Germany and Poland 1974-2024, as tabulated by the Federal Institute for Population Research (BiB) (https://www.bib.bund.de/DE/Fakten/Fakt/M13-Zuzuege-Fortzuege-Deutschland-Polen-ab-1974.html)
bases.m: People registered as moving between the country and Poland, all citizenships, summed over the calendar years of the period. Gross counts of all registered moves with no minimum stay: arrivals include ethnic German resettlers and Poles passing through, departures include Germans moving to Poland and Poles going home, and departures are under-recorded. 1990 is West Germany only. Eurostat's German series is about half of this from 2014 (probably its 12-month rule), and results from 2016 are only partly comparable with earlier years.

bases.s: ISTAT, Migration (transfer of residence): immigrants by country of origin (28_185_DF_DCIS_MIGRAZIONI_3) and emigrants by country of next residence (28_185_DF_DCIS_MIGRAZIONI_6), 2002-2024, Poland, https://esploradati.istat.it/SDMXWS/rest/data/28_185_DF_DCIS_MIGRAZIONI_3/
bases.m: People registered as moving between the country and Poland, all citizenships, summed over the calendar years of the period. Gross counts of registrations from abroad and cancellations to abroad in the municipal registers, all citizenships: immigrants include Italians returning from Poland, emigrants include Poles going home. Registrations are not only new arrivals: 2003 (10,973) and 2007 (19,246) are far above the neighbouring years, probably because Poles already living in Italy registered (the 2002 regularisation, the EU-citizen registration rules), which I did not verify; people who leave without cancelling their registration are missed.

bases.s: ABS, Overseas Migration 2022-23 (tables 2.1, 3.1, 1.1), financial years to 2022-23
bases.m: Overseas migrant arrivals of Poland-born people to Australia, summed over the financial years of the period. Arrivals are people who stay 12 of the next 16 months, so they include temporary migrants and returning residents, and did not necessarily come from Poland.

bases.s: Eurostat, first residence permits by citizenship (migr_resfirst, Poland), reuse with attribution
bases.m: First residence permits issued to non-EU citizens, all validities, summed over the calendar years of the period (2020-2024 covers five years).
bases.w: Permits are not arrivals: one person can receive several, permits valid under a year dominate, and refugees and EU citizens are largely missing.

bases.s: Eurostat, first residence permits by citizenship (migr_resfirst, Poland), reuse with attribution
bases.m: First residence permits issued to non-EU citizens that are valid 12 months or longer, summed over the calendar years of the period (2020-2024 covers five years).
